name: Slovenia
summary_text: Slovenia is among Central and Eastern Europe's most progressive destinations for trans visitors, with a cleaner documented profile than its neighbours. Legal gender recognition is depathologised (no surgery or psychiatric-diagnosis requirement), and a 2022 reform abolished local jurisdiction in the gender-change procedure — reducing involuntary outing through local bureaucracy. Comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers gender identity, same-sex marriage is legal (2022, via the Constitutional Court), and no far-right party is in government. No severe traveler-axis incidents surfaced in research: no mob violence against trans people, no trans-tourist rape, no European Court case of police abuse, and no documented foreign-trans-detention case — unlike several neighbours (Greece's Thessaloniki mob, Italy's tourist-rape and Milan police beating, Czechia's trans-foreigner extradition mishandling, Poland's foreign-trans-woman-in-male-detention). The main caveats are a far-right youth campaign ("Two Sexes, One Truth"), an underreporting/trust gap in hate-crime reporting, and thinner detention-placement evidence for a small country.

sources.title: Slovenia | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): one of the most progressive countries in Central and Eastern Europe - comprehensive anti-discrimination law since 2016 (Protection Against Discrimination Act, Advocate of the Principle of Equality); first post-Communist country to legalise same-sex marriage (2022 Constitutional Court ruling; effective January 2023 with joint adoption); legal gender recognition possible but lacks a clear, modern legal framework.

sources.title: Slovenia - F&M Global Barometers
sources.claim_summary: F&M Global Barometers country profile for Slovenia: composite LGBT-rights perception scores including the Global Barometer of Transgender Rights index.

sources.title: Termination of local jurisdiction in the procedure of gender change data | GOV.SI
sources.claim_summary: Slovenian Ministry of the Interior (Oct 2022): terminated local jurisdiction in gender-change procedures - trans people no longer exposed to involuntary disclosure of their trans identity in their local environment; procedures may now take place at any administrative unit; 157 gender reassignments entered in the civil register since 2005 (31 in 2022).

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Slovenia: police failed to intervene in attacks around the Pride march and discouraged reporting; Legebitra documented 17 cases and TransAkcija 25 cases of direct bias-motivated speech in 2023; an emergency parliamentary meeting concluded the ministry should adopt a national action plan.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Slovenia: courts recognised LGBTI asylum seekers' vulnerabilities; a journalist was ruled to have violated the journalists' code for portraying gender reassignment as commercialised and harmful; SDS and NSi proposed criminalising 'promotion' of homosexuality/trans identities (up to 3 years) mirroring Hungary/Russia laws - swiftly rejected by the government; a magazine special edition pushed anti-trans narratives; NSi proposed removing gender-affirming surgery from health coverage.

sources.title: Slovenia - United States Department of State
sources.claim_summary: US State Department 2023 Human Rights Practices report for Slovenia (archived): official assessment including treatment of LGBTI persons.

Peace Institute ENACT national report (Jan 2025): 'Enhancing the capacity of civil society organisations to support victims of anti-LGBTQI hate crimes' - Slovenia's legal and political context on anti-LGBTI hate crimes, part of an EU-funded six-country project.

sources.title: Slovenia passes same-sex marriage law - B92
sources.claim_summary: B92 (July 2006): Slovenia passed a same-sex marriage law but with restrictions - ceremonies limited to the two partners and a registration official, no friends or relatives, only in a state office; gay and lesbian organisations welcomed the step but criticised the law as 'insufficient'.

Inquirer/AFP (Dec 2015): Pope Francis urged Slovenian politicians to 'support the family' four days before the referendum on the gay-marriage law adopted by parliament in March - the referendum (later lost) followed a conservative challenge.
